en: *The Commentary on the Meaning of the Three-Limbed Syllogism* Established by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Xuanzang;
Composed by Yan-shou, Abbot of Yongming Temple.
The *Zhēn wéishí liàng* (The True Proof of Consciousness-Only) was excerpted by the Śramaṇa Mingyù of Western Shu.
This proof was presented by the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang at Kanyākubja in Central India,

during the eighteen-day *aviśeṣa-mahāpariṣad* (unrestricted great assembly) convened by King Śīlāditya, which widely summoned those from the five regions of India who were learned in the principles of the Dharma.
He set forth a formal syllogism (*prayoga*) as an adversary against the śramaṇas, brahmins, and even the followers of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhist paths;
this was inscribed upon a golden tablet. For eighteen days, not a single person dared to refute it.

According to his biography, the Great Master’s fame resounded throughout the Five Indias. A King named Kumāra of East India sent letters three times to the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra, desiring to welcome him to serve as a state preceptor.
The first letter stated: "Your disciple wishes to see the Great Virtuous One of China.
I beg the Master to send him here to comfort me with his esteemed favor. The second stated: "I earnestly pray that you will deign to look upon me; do not refuse my request again."
[The King] refused. Second, he did not reply to the letter. Third, he sent a letter saying: "I, your disciple, an ordinary person, am fickle in my joys and angers.
Having heard the name of a foreign monk, my body and mind were filled with joy, and I earnestly sought to meet him face-to-face.
If you do not come again, I shall surely become an evil man; I fear that my former defilements will arise once more. Furthermore, I shall mobilize my elephant army to trample the Nālandā Monastery."
"Shattered like dust. These words are as true as the sun; you, Master, should examine this well. When Dharma Master Śīlabhadra received the letter, he said to Master Xuanzang:

"That king’s virtuous mind has always been thin. Moreover, since the Buddha-dharma has not yet spread extensively within his realm, he has conceived a profound aspiration merely upon hearing your name.
If you do not go in accordance with his wishes, there may be demonic obstacles. It is appropriate that you comply; do not..."

Fearing the slight labor, Master Xuanzang complied with the command. He took his leave of his teacher and traveled together with the envoys. Upon meeting the King, he was received with great joy at first sight.
The King invited him into the inner palace and provided him with offerings for over a month.

When King Śīlāditya learned of this, he dispatched an envoy to King Kumāra, instructing him to send the Chinese monk immediately. The King [Kumāra] replied: "My head may be obtained, but the Dharma Master cannot."
King Śīlāditya was enraged and sent another messenger with a reprimand, saying: "If your head can be obtained, deliver it immediately to my envoy.
King Kumāra, deeply fearing that his words had led him astray, immediately ordered twenty thousand elephant divisions and thirty thousand naval vessels to set out together with the Master.
They traveled up the Ganges River to reach the King’s location. When the King reached the border, he went out to welcome the Master, feeling profound joy.

He personally presented exquisite delicacies, performed music, and scattered flowers. He further requested, saying, "I have heard that you, Master, have composed a treatise refuting wrong views; where is it?
Master Xuanzang immediately produced the formal syllogisms (*prayoga*) he had established and presented them to the King. Upon examining them, the King rejoiced and praised them incessantly.
Thereafter, he showed them throughout to his hundred officials as well as all those of pure conduct. He then said to the Master, "This formulation is most correct."

The disciples and their masters were all convinced and submitted. However, [the Master] reflected that other small-vehicle (Hīnayāna) schools and non-Buddhists (tīrthika) in neighboring kingdoms still clung to ignorance and delusion.

He wished to convene a great assembly at Kanyākubja, gathering scholars from various countries so that the Dharma Master’s profound discourse could be established and accepted by both opponents and proponents alike, thereby gaining the trust of the contemporary world. What do you think of this, Master? The Dharma Master approved, and so...
Having heard that various kingdoms had fixed the date for the assembly, Master Xuanzang and the King traveled upstream along the Ganges from the beginning of winter;
it was not until the end of the twelfth month that they arrived at the venue.
There were already eighteen kings of the Five Indias, over three thousand monks of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and over two thousand Brahmins and Nirgrantha heretics.
More than a thousand monks from Nālandā Monastery had already gathered for some time;

all were masters of extensive learning and textual meaning, endowed with abundant eloquence, and they had come to this assembly desiring to hear the sound of the Dharma. Accompanying them were attendants, elephant carriages, and colorful banners, rising like clouds and surging like mist.
This was such that even the "Six Qi" [dynasty] could not match the sleeves joined together to form a canopy, nor could the "Three Wu" [region] compare to the sweat falling like rain. Even so—
When the festival reached its peak, the King completed the arrangement of all the food vessels and implements for both the inner and outer circles.
He specially prepared a jeweled throne and invited Master Xuanzang to sit upon it as the presiding debater (*vādin*), extolling the Mahāyāna and explaining the purpose of composing the treatise.

He further requested that Dharma Master Śīlabhadra read the text aloud for the great assembly. A separate copy was transcribed and hung outside the gate. This continued for eighteen days without interruption.
A person came forward to debate. The King lifted Master Xuanzang’s *kāṣāya* robe and proclaimed aloud:
"The Dharma Master from China has established the principles of the Mahāyāna and refuted all heterodox views. Since the eighteenth day, no one has dared to debate him. You should take this to heart.
The entire assembly rejoiced, and they all hailed Master Xuanzang as the "Celestial Being of the Mahāyāna."
Thus, the *Yinming shu* (Commentary on the Logic of Valid Cognition) states:

"For example, when the Great Master had completed his travels throughout the Western Regions and was about to return with his studies fulfilled, King Śīlāditya—who ruled over the five regions of India—organized an eighteen-day *aviśeṣa-mahāpariṣad* (unrestricted great assembly). He commanded the Master to establish his propositions (*siddhānta*).

From all across India, the most learned and virtuous were selected and gathered at the site of the assembly. He then dispatched non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and followers of the Hīnayāna to compete in raising challenges and interrogations."
When the Great Master established his formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*), no one dared to challenge or respond to it.
This citation from Dharma Master Ji’s *Commentary on the Nyāyamukha* serves to corroborate the aforementioned matter.

Indeed, when the Great Master established his syllogism, it was as if the sun had already risen, causing the light of fireflies and candles to be eclipsed; consequently, those followers of heterodox paths who sought to disrupt the orthodoxy were rendered powerless.

Those who are tongue-tied and swallow their words, who cling to the literal text while doubting its underlying principle, must cease their debate and contemplate deeply; is this not due to the power of *hetuvidyā* (logic)?

The Great Master established the following *vīśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-pramāṇa* (inference based on specific characteristics): "The color that is truly and universally acknowledged is the *dharmin* (the subject); it is certainly not separate from the eye."
The proponent of the thesis [identifies] the reason as: "because it is admitted by oneself to be included within the first three [bases] while not being included among those subsumed under the eye.

The concordant example is "like the visual consciousness," and the combined statement is: "whatever is included within the first three bases and is not included among those subsumed under the eye does not exist apart from visual consciousness;
the concordant example is like visual consciousness, and the discordant example is like the visual faculty."
The four characters "because it is real" (*tattvataḥ*) are words used to set aside objections by way of a formal statement; this will be explained below.
The single character "form" (*rūpa*) is precisely the *dharmin* (the subject); presenting the *dharmin* first is termed the "basis of the thesis" (*pakṣāśraya*).

The phrase "certainly not separate from visual consciousness" is the "body of the thesis" (*pakṣatattva*), which constitutes the *dharma* (predicate) to be established for the *dharmin* of form, as one investigates that form in its original nature as the self-cognition of visual consciousness.

Regarding the "divisions that are transformations": since they arise from the transformation of consciousness, they are fundamentally not separate from consciousness. Therefore, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is established as: "They are certainly not separate from eye-consciousness. The reason (*hetu*) is stated as:

"Because, according to your own admission, they are included within the first three [categories] yet are not included by the eye [organ]. This is called the "proving property" (*sādhana-dharma*), which serves as the reason.
That is to say, the thesis to be established is that "form is not separate from consciousness"; thus, the reason for this thesis excludes only the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

This clarifies the meaning that visible form is not separate from consciousness. "Inclusion" (saṃgraha) means "to hold. This refers to the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—each of which has six elements (*dhātu*).
Regarding the statement "included in the first three," this takes, for instance, the three elements belonging to the eye: the eye, visible form, and eye-consciousness.

That which is not included by the eye refers to what the eye-faculty does not grasp, because eye-consciousness does not see the eye-faculty itself; this is admitted as being separate. Only two elements are taken [as included], because...
"Manifest color and consciousness are not separate; the analogy is like visual consciousness" means that when the eye—the seeing portion—perceives color, it directly grasps the essence of the color.

This is the sense of "not being separate. It serves as an analogy for the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) within the thesis [of the visual consciousness], which is not separate from the color that it has transformed.
The phrase "combined, as stated below" refers to the formation of the body of the thesis. In this combination, the reason comes first, followed by the thesis, and then the example is cited.
The negative example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is established according to the formal structure of inference (*anumāna*). Regarding the phrase "like the eye-faculty" (*cakṣur-indriya*):

this refers to an eye-faculty that is not subsumed by consciousness within the context of the reason (*hetu*). It carries the sense of being "separated," because consciousness does not perceive the eye-faculty itself.

In contrast to the positive example (*sādharmya*), where the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—specifically the visual consciousness of form (*rūpa-vijñāna*)—are all inseparable, it is therefore called the "negative example. If sound, odor, taste, or touch were...
The basis of the thesis (*pakṣa*) consists of the subject (*dharmin*), the thesis itself (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*).

The selection of the properties (*dharma*) is the same as before. Question: Why is the phrase "admitted by oneself" (*svayam-abhyupagata*) not included? Answer: It is not a correct reason (*hetu*); rather, it is merely a preliminary statement used at the beginning of the reason to exclude fallacies.
Furthermore, it is not that the Hīnayāna does not admit it while the Mahāyāna admits it; for the reason operates upon the subject (*dharmin*), and all three members [of the syllogism] are likewise.
Because this is common [to both systems].
According to the Mahāyāna school, it is admitted that there are physical forms (*rūpa*) of Buddhas in other directions;

therefore, the phrase "admitted by oneself" is placed at the beginning of the reason (*hetu*) to exclude the fault of a contradictory particularity (*viśeṣa-viruddha*) within the property-bearer (*dharmin*). Thus, it is said: "Nor is it not [the case] for the Hīnayāna."

[The opponent] grants [this]. The Mahāyāna itself grants it, because the reason—"being subsumed by the first three [elements] while not being subsumed by the eye"—is accepted by both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.

As for the statement that "the reason operates upon the locus (*dharmin*) and all three members are common," this means that the reason, the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are all common [to both schools].

It is not the case that [the reason] necessarily operates in separation from visual consciousness and visible form, nor does it necessarily operate simultaneously with visual consciousness and visible form. This is...
Because there is the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the phrase "as admitted by oneself" (*svābhyupagama*) is employed to exclude this fault.

The first section clarifies the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*); the latter provides the questions and answers. The initial passage has two parts: first, the demonstration of the thesis; second, the explanation of the reason.

Regarding the former, the words of the subject (*dharmin*) are the five characters: "because it is real, the color-form (*rūpa*) as commonly established. Among these, the single character "color-form" (*rūpa*) is precisely the property-bearer (*dharmin*).

The remaining four characters merely serve to prevent errors. Specifically, the first two characters, "truly" (zhen) and "because" (gu), prevent errors such as contradicting worldly conventions and contradicting the teachings.
I shall now explain *anumāna* (inference). First, I will provide a topical outline (*prakaraṇa*) to clarify the structure of the chapter.
Regarding the initial statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the term "form" (*rūpa*) is established as the subject (*dharmin*) of the proposition; all other elements serve to prevent logical fallacies.
Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "because it is real," there are two types of faults to be excluded, which will be explained in the subsequent text.
The opponent asks: "In the mundane world, which is shallow and superficial, it is known through direct perception that form exists apart from consciousness.

Now, the Mahāyāna posits that form is not separate from visual consciousness because this is not what is commonly known in the world. Why does this inference not incur the fallacy of contradicting worldly consensus? Answer: "In establishing an inference, there are three types:
those based on one's own [perspective], those based on another's, and those based on what is common to both. Each of these applies according to its respective context."

Regarding the exclusions: if it is a *svārthānumāna* (inference for oneself), the term "asserted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*) serves as the exclusion; if it is a *parārthānumāna* (inference for others), the term "maintained by you" (*bhavataḥ parigṛhīta*) serves as the exclusion;

if it is a *sādhāraṇānumāna* (common inference), the term "ultimately" (*paramārthatas*) serves as the exclusion. Now, in this case of common inference, there is a specific distinction: the phrase "because it is true" (*satyatvāt*) indicates that [the object] relies upon the ultimate.
That is to say, among the four types of ultimate truths, it is established based on the truth of the manifestation of essence and function (*tattva-kārya-prabhāsana-satya*).
This question addresses the fault of contradicting worldly convention. The answer uses the term "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) for the sake of exclusion.
By stating "four kinds of ultimate," it excludes the four kinds of conventional (*saṃvṛti*). The four conventions are: first, worldly convention, such as jars, basins, armies, and forests;
second, rational convention, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); third, the convention of realization...

This refers to the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and so forth. The four conventional establishments (*vyavasthāna-saṃvṛti*) refer to the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*). Regarding the four ultimate truths (*paramārtha*):

first, the truth of the manifestation of essence and function (*tattva-kārya-prabhāsa-satya*), which refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth. Because they possess a substantial nature that transcends the initial conventional level, they are called "ultimate.

Because they are designated according to their specific distinctions as "aggregates" and so forth, and because each possesses its own activity, they are termed "manifestation. Second, the cause... [text continues]
The truth of the differentiation of fruits refers to suffering, its origin, and so forth—the differentiation of cause and effect regarding wisdom, abandonment, realization, and cultivation.

The third is the truth of reality revealed through the gateway of the three bases, which refers to the principle of the two kinds of emptiness. Because it transcends the conventional and is realized, it is called the ultimate (paramārtha). It is based on emptiness that one is able to realize it.

Because it reveals the reality, it is called the "entrance of reliance. Fourth is the truth of setting aside the expression to discuss the ultimate meaning, which refers to the single True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Its essence is wondrous and transcends words, and is thus already termed the "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*). Now, regarding the first sense [of this term], because the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses each possess their own essence and function that manifest as meanings.
Question: It may be so that not contradicting the world does not constitute being "non-learned" (aśaikṣa).

Furthermore, since the World-Honored One also permitted in the Hīnayāna Āgamas that form exists apart from consciousness, and since the Hīnayāna learners collectively reckon that there are real objects external to the mind, would this not contradict the teachings of the Āgamas and other scriptures?
Hīnayāna Learner: This is established solely based on the superior meaning of the Mahāyāna; it does not [contradict the Āgamas].
To contravene the teachings of the Hīnayāna is a worldly failing for those who study.

Furthermore, when questioned regarding such faults as contradicting the scriptures, he likewise answers with brevity by stating that [the object] is real. The Buddha taught that form exists apart from consciousness.

Originally, he was of limited capacity. Having attained an understanding of the emptiness of the substrate (*āśraya*) in relation to adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*), he was taught that the mind and its objects are dualistic.

He had not yet realized that the mutual perception of subject and object is fundamentally empty; thus, he did not speak of the non-duality of mind and object. Now, we rely upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Question: While the phrase "because it is real" excludes faults such as contradicting worldly consensus or scriptural authority, what fault does the two-word term "universally established" (*prasiddha*) exclude?
Answer: By employing the term "universally established," one excludes two types of forms that are not universally established. Among the twenty schools of the Hīnayāna, [one must] exclude...

The Ekavyāvahārikas, the Lokottaravādins, the Prajñaptivādins, and the Kukkulikas—these four schools, along with the remaining sixteen, all maintain that the final-body Bodhisattva possesses defiled form (*rūpa*) and that the Buddha possesses out-flowing form (*sāsrava-rūpa*). The Mahāyāna does not accept this;

thus, these are forms that are not universally established (*aprasiddha*). The Mahāyāna asserts that Buddhas of other directions possess form and that the Buddha possesses out-flow-free form (*anāsrava-rūpa*). Although the Sautrāntikas...
While they allow for the form (*rūpa*) of Buddhas from other realms, they do not allow it to be untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, the other nineteen schools do not allow for its existence;
thus, along with the two aforementioned types of form that are not universally established (*aprasiddha*), [it remains unaccepted].

This concludes the preceding statement regarding "because it is true," which merely excludes faults such as contradicting the teachings concerning the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the thesis (*pakṣa*). It further asks:

what fault does the phrase "universally acknowledged" (*prasiddha*) exclude? The answer is: by the term "universally acknowledged," one excludes matter (*rūpa*) that is not universally acknowledged by both schools;
this excludes the error of contradicting the tenet regarding the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*). As for the twenty schools: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, more than a hundred years...
In the [X]th year, the Great Assembly of the Buddha’s Dharma was first split (*bheda*, meaning division) due to the Dragon Elephant (*nāga-hastin*).

Because of differences regarding the five topics—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*—discussed by the fourfold assembly of learned and virtuous elders, they divided into two schools:
first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Sthavira. From the Mahāsāṃghika, eight schools branched out. Together...
The fundamental schools are nine in number: first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Ekavyāvahārika;
third, the Lokottaravādin; fourth, the Kaukkuṭika; fifth, the Bahuśrutīya; sixth, the Prajñaptivādin; seventh, the Caitika; eighth, the Aparaseliya;
and ninth, the Uttaraseliya. From the Sthavira school, two divisions were formed: the Sarvāstivāda and [the Vātsīputrīya].
The second is the Sthavira school, which changed its name to the Haimavata school. From the Sarvāstivāda school, nine schools were successively derived;
together with the two original root schools, they constitute eleven schools. First is the Sarvāstivāda school.
2. Haimavata; 3. Vātsīputrīya; 4. Dharmottarīya; 5. Bhadrayānīya; 6. Saṃmitīya; 7. Prajñaptivādin;
8. Mahīśāsaka; 9. Dharmaguptaka; 10. Kāśyapīya; 11. Sautrāntika.
Together with the preceding nine schools, these constitute twenty schools. Excluding the four schools beginning with the Ekavyāvahārika, the remainder...
Regarding the sixteen schools that assert that a Bodhisattva possesses defiled matter (*kliṣṭa-rūpa*) and that a Buddha possesses out-flowing matter (*sāsrava-rūpa*), the Sarvāstivādins state:
"An Arhat still experiences the results of past karma; the liberation of a Buddha and that of the two vehicles [Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] are no different.

One should say that a Bodhisattva is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) whose fetters (*saṃyojana*) have not yet been severed. This is their position concerning the Bodhisattva’s possession of defiled matter and the Buddha’s possession of out-flowing matter.

Regarding the mind associated with outflowing form (*sāsrava-rūpa*): the Sautrāntikas do not admit that the Buddha possesses outflowing form. Their position on this largely accords with that of the Sarvāstivādins;
these views are all accepted by the Hīnayāna, whereas they are not accepted by the Mahāyāna. As for what the Mahāyāna does accept:
The Hīnayāna does not accept this; therefore, the term "universally established" (*prasiddha*) is included to exclude these two types of non-universally established forms.

If the term "universally established" were not stated, and one were to simply say that "true form" is the subject (*dharmin*), then the thesis (*pakṣa*) would necessarily be that it is not separate from visual consciousness.

Furthermore, when discussing "form" (rūpa), whether it is accepted or not accepted, it is entirely subsumed within the category of the "dharmin" (the subject possessing properties). That which was accepted by the Hinayana previously is not accepted by the Mahayana;
if one now establishes it as "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra), one commits the fallacy of the "partial non-establishment of the specific property of the subject" (ekadeśasvadharmyasiddha).
Furthermore, one incurs the fault of violating a portion of the teachings. Moreover, that which is permitted in the Mahāyāna is not permitted in the Hīnayāna;
yet now, one establishes it as an existent phenomenon (*dharmin*), thereby incurring the fault of the "unestablishedness of the specific" (*asiddha-viśeṣa*) for one party.

When one subsequently adduces the reason "because it is included in the first three [aggregates] but not included in the eye," one then incurs the fault of the "unestablishedness of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for either oneself or the other party, as the subject (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not established.
Because form (*rūpa*) serves as the basis [for the definition], all four types are now excluded; thus, the term "established by consensus" (*prasiddha*) is employed.
Once the exclusion denoted by the two characters "established by consensus" is completed, all other forms are fully accomplished; this is what is meant by "established by consensus.
If either the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna schools does not accept it, this constitutes the fallacy of being unestablished with respect to the qualified object (*viśeṣya-asiddha*).

Therefore it is said: If one does not state "universally established" (*prasiddha*) but merely says "because it is real, [it is] form, etc.," then both the forms that were previously accepted and those not accepted—which carry faults—would be entirely included within the *dharmin* (the subject) "form.
By what means could one then distinguish between them? In the passage below, it clarifies that two types of fallacies are committed:
by establishing as "consciousness-only" a form that one's own Mahāyāna school does not accept, one commits the fallacy of contradicting one's own [tenets].
One would incur the fault of the object of qualification (*viśeṣya*) being unestablished for one party, and also commit the error of contradicting one's own school regarding a portion of the thesis.

Furthermore, in the section on the Mahāyāna, it means that if one posits as "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) that which is not admitted by the Hīnayāna, one commits the fault of the object of qualification being unestablished for one party.
As for the phrase "down to the following," it refers to the point when the reason (*hetu*) is adduced to establish the body of the thesis (*pakṣa*). In total...
If one were to include colors that are not admitted by either oneself or the other, one would incur the fault of the basis being unestablished for at least one of the two parties.
Since a basis that is not established for both cannot serve as a foundation, these four faults cannot be avoided.
By now employing the two qualifying terms "admitted" (*prasiddha*) and "mutually" (*ubhaya*), these four types of faults are excluded.

Question: Regarding the two characters "extremely established" (*ji cheng*), they exclude those forms that are not extremely established for both schools. I do not yet understand which forms the Tripitaka Master posits as being "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). Answer:
Excluding those forms that are not extremely established for both schools, all other forms accepted by both the proponent and the opponent are taken collectively as being consciousness-only.
Therefore, the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Inmyeong so) states: "Establishing all forms accepted [by both sides], remaining after the two [unestablished] categories, as being consciousness-only."
Because it is consciousness.
This was already distinguished previously; he asks again: "By what kind of form (*rūpa*) is [the world] established as representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*)? He answers:
"Except for the two types that are not universally accepted, all other forms are established by universal consensus. Below this, he cites scriptural authority to establish the remaining forms.
This constitutes the meaning of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). The above concludes the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Now follows the statement of the reason (*hetu*): "It certainly does not function apart from the eye. This is the well-established qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Question:

Why does this not incur the fault of the qualifier being unestablished (*asiddha*)? For instance, among the Śrāvakas (Hīnayāna), who would admit that form (*rūpa*) does not exist apart from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*)? Answer: In this context, it is indeed established.
This is the basis for our own school’s doctrine; however, this meaning of "not being separate" can also be established within other schools.

This is because the Hīnayāna admits that visual consciousness takes form as its object and directly apprehends its essence, which possesses the sense of "not being separate. Furthermore, they also admit that the visual consciousness itself is not separate from the visual consciousness.
Therefore, there is no fault of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) being unestablished (*aprasiddha*).

Having cited the body of the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established within the inference, it is shown that the qualifier is indeed established. Furthermore, a question-and-answer session is presented to clarify the intent of establishing the thesis;
namely, that the Hīnayāna does not admit that form (*rūpa*) is not separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is what is being established.
The thesis that "it is not separate from visual consciousness" is not universally established (*aprasiddha*). The meaning of the response is as follows:

When the Hīnayāna asserts that form is separate from visual consciousness, "form" serves as the subject (*dharmin*) of the inference; however, this has not yet been integrated with the actual thesis (*pakṣa*), and thus there is no specific qualification.

This is because the Hīnayāna merely infers based on objective form (*dravyarūpa*), and therefore claims it is separate from consciousness. The Mahāyāna, however, intends to accept that this is representational form (*nimittabhāga-rūpa*).
Therefore, they are certainly not separate. However, the passage beginning with "But he... clarifies that within the Hīnayāna school there is the principle of non-separation;

thus, one may establish a thesis by applying the words to their underlying meaning. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, they admit... means that the Hīnayāna admits that visual consciousness has the fundamental existence (*bhāva*) as its essence and the apprehension of form (*rūpa*) as its function.
Since it does not depart from its essence when apprehending form, even when it does not apprehend form, it likewise does not depart from its function. That...

Since both parties have agreed that they are not separate, the thesis that [the eye] is definitely not separate from visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) is established; thus, there is no fault of the qualifier being unestablished (aprasiddha).
Question: Since it is admitted that visual consciousness perceives its object, color (rūpa), and that there is a sense of non-separation, this should subsequently constitute the body of the thesis.
Is there mutual support [between the thesis and its reason]? Answer: There is no fault of mutual support. In the Mahāyāna, one merely takes the object as not being separate from the mind;

there is no real external object. If the proponent establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*) by combining the preceding and subsequent terms, and the proponent accepts it while the opponent does not, this mutual contention between the proponent and the opponent is called the essence of the thesis (*pakṣatattva*).
Herein, they contend only over the verbal expression (*vacana*), without yet having inferred the intended implication (*abhiprāya*). This is the definition.

[The] thesis [is] concluded. [The] meaning of the question is as follows: the Hīnayāna school maintains the principle of non-separation; the Mahāyāna establishes the thesis that [the object] is definitely not separate from visual consciousness.

This constitutes the fault of mutual contradiction. [The] meaning of the answer is as follows: the Mahāyāna speaks thus in order to clarify the tenet of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Therefore, it says:

There are no objects external to the mind. If one combines the preceding and succeeding propositions to establish a point of contention between proponent and opponent, this constitutes the essence of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Since that [proposition] is established solely by inferring and clarifying it upon the basis of substantial form (*dravyarūpa*), it is said that "only the verbally expressed is contested.
Because it has not yet clarified the Mahāyāna’s intended admission of the aspectual form (*nimittabhāga-rūpa*), it is said that "the intended admission has not yet been inferred."

Next, regarding the explanation of the cause, there are two parts: first, clarifying the primary cause; second, employing provisional terminology to eliminate errors. First, concerning the statement that the primary cause is "subsumed by the first three":
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), this refers to the first element of each of the three groups of six.

These are the eye faculty element (*cakṣur-indriya-dhātu*), the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*), and the form-object element (*rūpa-viṣaya-dhātu*). These are the first three elements within the eighteen elements.
To explain this cause, I shall first provide a topical outline to clarify the sequence and present a detailed analysis. First, regarding the explanation of the first half of the cause:
"The eighteen elements" (*dhātu*) refers to the three categories of sense-faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Each of these three has six factors;

as each of the six maintains its own distinct domain, they are called "elements. These are the six faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and the six [objects]—form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.

Regarding "dust" (viṣaya): consciousness follows the sense organs (indriya) and the dust; thus, it also has six names. All of these take the first member of each triad: for the organ, one takes the eye-organ element (cakṣur-indriya-dhātu);
for the dust, one takes the form-dust element (rūpa-viṣaya-dhātu); and for consciousness, one takes the eye-consciousness element (cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu).
Therefore, it is said that these are the first three elements among the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu).

Question: Even if one does not say "subsumed under the first three [aggregates]," but merely says "not subsumed by the eye," what further fault is there? Answer: There are two faults: first, the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
second, the fault of contradicting one's own teaching (*svaśāstravirodha*). Regarding the fault of being inconclusive:

if one were to formulate a syllogism as follows—"That which is truly established as form (*rūpa*) is necessarily not separate from visual consciousness; the reason (*hetu*) is that it is 'not subsumed by the eye'; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like visual consciousness itself. |||

The reason "not being subsumed by the eye" is too broad (*vyabhicāra*). It applies to the latter three among the five [sense organs] following the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*), because all of them are likewise not subsumed by the eye.
Consequently, the opponent points out the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), asking:

"Is it like visual consciousness—which, while not subsumed by the eye, is nevertheless inseparable from visual consciousness—that you intend to prove that 'manifest color' (*rūpa*) is inseparable from visual consciousness? Or is it like the latter three among the five [organs], which are also [not subsumed by the eye]?"

[It is] not included [in those categories]. Since the latter five [consciousnesses] are established in three meditative absorptions as being dissociated from eye-consciousness, does this not prove that the color-form (*rūpa*) you accept as established is indeed dissociated from eye-consciousness?
Question: In the Mahāyāna, is it not maintained that the latter five [consciousnesses] and the three [absorptions] are likewise not dissociated from eye-consciousness? Answer:

Even if the Mahāyāna were to concede that the latter five and the three are not dissociated from eye-consciousness, while avoiding the fault of an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*), it would nonetheless contradict its own tenets (*svasiddhānta*). This is because, according to the Mahāyāna school...

Because it is stated that the latter five [elements] are dissociated from the three types of consciousness and from eye-consciousness, the first three [elements] are established as encompassing half of the causes. This excludes the latter five and the three [of the former], as they are not subsumed within the first three.
Since the causes consist of both the latter half and the former half, when combined, they achieve perfection without fault; were even one of these missing, the assembly would be incomplete.

A fallacy arises here. Therefore, the Master of the Treatise (the *śāstrin*) employs a dialogue to clarify the details. If one does not state [the reason] below, the dialogue would fail to reveal the fallacy;

furthermore, "and not being determinate" (*aniyata*) below indicates the three members of the syllogism. Immediately following "that is," the fallacy of the incomplete reason (*ardha-hetu*) is pointed out.

Under "by the opponent" (*bahir-anga*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is established: "Is it like visual consciousness? This refers to visual consciousness as the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). It is that which is not perceived by the eye...
"Subsumption" refers to the fact that the faculties and consciousnesses are each distinct. "Eye-consciousness is not separate from eye-consciousness" means that,
using the example of eye-consciousness, one demonstrates that the subject (*dharmin*) of the thesis—
form (*rūpa*), which is already established— is likewise not separate from the predicate (*dharma*) of the thesis, eye-consciousness, just as in the case of the subsequent [example].
The "five triads" below present a contradictory measure (*pramāṇa*) to demonstrate that the reason (*hetu*) possesses the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
As for the latter five triads—namely, those of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—each consists of a triad of faculty, object, and consciousness. These are also not subsumed under the eye;

that is to say, the three realms of the latter five are distinct from the first three realms, and therefore they are likewise not subsumed. The three [realms] of the latter five are necessarily separate from the eye.

Regarding "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): it refers to the fact that within the last five [realms], the three [realms of smell, taste, and touch], and the first three realms of consciousness (*dhātu*), eye-consciousness is invariably absent.
This serves as a proof that the "color-form" (*rūpa*) established by you is definitively separate from eye-consciousness.

By using the last five, three, and first three realms as a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), one proves that just as they are invariably separate from eye-consciousness, so too is the color-form established by you definitively separate from eye-consciousness. Thus, this reason (*hetu*) occurs in both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances.

This constitutes the fallacy of the "inconclusive" (anaikāntika). Question: Regarding the passage beginning with "Now, in the Mahāyāna," the intention is that since it is established that all phenomena are consciousness-only, it is certain that the latter three of the five [factors] do not exist apart from consciousness.
Therefore, the response says: "Even if one were to grant that they are not separate [from consciousness], one avoids committing the fallacy of the inconclusive."
This would contradict one's own school’s tenets, for the Mahāyāna school asserts that the latter three [of the six consciousnesses] are distinct from eye-consciousness.

Question: If one merely states that they are subsumed under the first three [aggregates], rather than stating that they are not subsumed by the eye, what fault is there? Answer: This also commits two faults: first, the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
second, the fault of contradiction with the determined specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha*) of the dharma. Regarding the inconclusive [fault]: if one were to establish...

The *pramāṇa* states: "Because it is truly established as form (*rūpa*), it is certainly not separate from visual consciousness. The reason (*hetu*) states: "Because it is included within the first three [bases]. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "Like visual consciousness.

Thus, the reason "being included within the first three" is too broad (*vyabhicāra*); it applies to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Consequently, an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) arises:

"Is it the case that, just as visual consciousness is included within the first three and is not separate from visual consciousness, so too is truly established form not separate from visual consciousness?"
Is it not the case that the eye-faculty is also included within the first three [aggregates], and that the eye-faculty is not necessarily inseparable from eye-consciousness?

Does this not prove your established position that form is not necessarily inseparable from eye-consciousness? Question: Why do you not say "necessarily inseparable," but instead say "not necessarily inseparable"?
Answer: Regarding the Mahāyāna eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) in relation to the eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), they are neither definitively identical nor separate.

First, as for why they are not separate: the faculty is the cause and consciousness is the effect; because they are simultaneous, they are not separate. Furthermore, because matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are distinct, they are said to be not identical. Thus, we simply say they are not definitively non-separate.
Second, regarding the fault of the self-characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the two transgressing dharmas being determined and contradictory: it is said that the dharma... [text fragment ends]

The "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*) stated last in the thesis (*pakṣa*). To say that there is a "definite contradiction" means that the reason (*hetu*) contradicts the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The opponent presents a syllogism of contradiction as follows: "Visible form, which is established as real, is the subject (*dharmin*); it is not the case that it is not inseparable from visual consciousness—this is the thesis (*sādhya*).
The reason is: because it is included within the first three [bases]. The example is: like the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Thus, the opponent employs this previous syllogism differently.
The "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) is treated as the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*).

That is to say, since the previous [argument] used only the latter part of the reason (*hetu*) and already committed two fallacies, what would be the fallacy if one were now to use only the former part of the reason?
Therefore, the answer states: "It likewise commits two fallacies. First, regarding the section on "indefiniteness" (*anaikāntika*), the three members [of the syllogism] are established as follows:
The third point below clarifies that there is the fallacy of uncertainty due to the cause. "As in the case of visual consciousness" (below) restates the certainty of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*);
that is, the visual consciousness used as the similar example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the visual consciousness included within the first three [categories].

Since the visual consciousness of the similar example is not separate from the subsequent term "visual consciousness," it proves that the established color (*rūpa*) is likewise not separate from the subsequent term "visual consciousness. "As in the case of the visual faculty" (below).
This restates the contradictory evidence to demonstrate that the reason (*hetu*) possesses the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

That is to say, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), which serves as the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), is also included within the category of "being subsumed by the first three [elements]. Since the faculties and consciousnesses are distinct, they are not necessarily inseparable;

therefore, it is said that the eye-faculty is not necessarily inseparable from the subsequent term, eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Thus, it proves that the established color-form (*rūpa*) is not necessarily inseparable from the subsequent term, eye-consciousness. This is because...

The first three [reasons] are subsumed under the "probans" (*hetu*). To function in both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is the fallacy of being "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

Question: Why does it not state that they are definitely separated from the lower? This is because, within the analysis of contradictory measures (*viruddha-pramāṇa*), there is no meaning of being definitely not separated.

Originally, regarding the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) in relation to the eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) in the Mahāyāna, there are two distinctions: namely, that they are neither definitely identical nor definitely separate; their cause and effect are simultaneous. This is...

It is not the meaning of being separate. That form and mind are distinct is the meaning of "not being identical. Therefore, regarding identity and separation, the statement that they are "not fixed" implies that the two meanings are interrelated.
Under the section on the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the two types of transgressions, the second type of fault is explained.

As for the opponent presenting a syllogism of contradiction: previously, the thesis established was that [the object] is definitely not separate from visual consciousness; now, by means of "non-... [it is refuted].

The thesis that "concentration is not separate from visual consciousness" is a contradictory meaning. In the previous formal argument (*pramāṇa*), the eye-faculty was used as the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*);

now, the eye-faculty is used as the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). This, too, is a contradiction. Since the dissimilar example has been converted into a similar example, it follows that the similar example can likewise become a dissimilar example.
Although both the thesis and the example thus possess the contradictions of similarity and dissimilarity, herein—

This merely demonstrates that the reason (*hetu*) cited in the first three [propositions] is too broad (*vyabhicāra*), and thus stands in definitive contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property to be proven (*dharmin*) stated in the subsequent thesis.

Question: Can there be a contradiction with the specific characteristic of the property to be proven? Answer: That would not constitute a genuine refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). For a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) that contradicts the specific characteristic of the property to be proven must satisfy the following conditions:

for the proponent, it must be non-existent in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and existent in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); whereas for the opponent, it must be existent in the similar instances and non-existent in the dissimilar instances. Only then does it establish a contradiction with the specific characteristic of the property to be proven.

This is contradictory. Since both the proponent and the opponent now possess both similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), this is not the fault of a "contradiction with the specific characteristic of the property" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddha*).

Question: Since it is not a contradiction with the specific characteristic of the property, can it still incur the fault of being "inconclusive due to a contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*)?

Answer: This is also not the case. Now, the fallacy of "contradiction" (*viruddha*) and "indefiniteness" (*anaikāntika*) occurs when the proponent and opponent dispute over a single *dharmin* (subject), yet their respective reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) differ, even though each possesses the three characteristics:
being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), being present in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and being entirely absent from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*).
However, because these reasons fail to produce correct cognition in one another, both parties remain in doubt and cannot definitively establish a single thesis; this is called "contradiction."

This is not the fallacy of the "contradictory-unsettled" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). Now, because [the subject] is real, it is established by both parties; although the "color" (*rūpa*) is a single property (*dharma*) that is the object of dispute, the reason (*hetu*) is nonetheless common to both.
Furthermore, since each [of the two reasons] lacks the third characteristic (*tṛtīya-lakṣaṇa*), it does not constitute the fallacy of the "contradictory-unsettled. Question:

Since this fallacy does not exist, why does the *Hetubindu-ṭīkā* state that one commits the fallacy of the "contradictory-to-the-own-characteristic" (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha-viruddhāvyabhicārin*)? Answer: It is merely...
This is the force of the Master’s free-flowing brushwork. It is distinguished from the previously mentioned "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) fallacy;

it is a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*) consisting of a "contradiction regarding the specific characteristic" (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha-vidhi*) and a "counter-balanced" (*pratipakṣita*) fallacy, as it is not truly existent.
Because this probans exists, the first three categories include "that which is not subsumed by the eye," thereby mutually excluding various inconclusive, contradictory, and other such fallacies.
This is essentially similar to *anumāna* (inference). There are thirty-three faults in total; fourteen of these pertain to the reason (*hetu*).

Because the names are identical while their meanings differ from those [previously discussed], the Master of the Treatise poses a question to distinguish between the authentic and the spurious. The section beginning with "The self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena" explains the first of the four types of contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*) in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*).
Regarding the phrase "identical in non-existence but different in existence," it refers to the proponent’s similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

"Without cause. "The dissimilar instance has a cause; while the similar instance has it, the dissimilar instance lacks it. This means that for the opponent, the similar instance possesses the reason (*hetu*), whereas the dissimilar instance lacks it.
Now, establishing this against the opponent, we explain that this fault is not genuine. "The similar example has it, the dissimilar example has it":
this means that both the similar and dissimilar examples take the first three [categories] as their collective reason. Question: Since it is not... [the argument] turns subtle.

"Another fallacy. From "Now, it is determined that... below, [the author] explains the sixth type of fallacy among the six types of *anaikāntika* (inconclusive) reasons in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*).

From "Now, because it is real... below, he shows that this fallacy is not genuine. Regarding the statement "each lacks the third characteristic," this means they lack the property of being entirely absent from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

Since the two factors—sense organs (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—are each taken as the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), there is no substance for a dissimilar instance; therefore, it is said that each lacks [the third characteristic].
Third. Question: Regarding the passage "Since there is no such fault... and below, [the author] explains the errors of the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* commentator (Sūzhǔ).
Because he follows the predecessors, he merely speaks of the momentum of his brushstrokes (*zòngbǐ zhī shì*).

As for the statement that the "common inconclusive" (*gòng bùding*) is distinguished from [the list], it is distinguished from the first type of fault among the six types of inconclusive reasons in *Hetuvidyā*. Since it is not a genuine fault, it is called "similar" (*xiāngsì*). There is.
Regarding this underlying cause: there are those who take only the first half or the second half as the cause, which results in these four faults.
Therefore, the cause of complete and perfect accomplishment is established to mutually exclude them.
Next, to clarify the use of the phrase "admitted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*) to avoid logical faults: Question: For what purpose is the phrase "admitted by oneself" employed at the beginning? Answer:

Because within the scope of the *Tripiṭaka*’s valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there exists the fault of contradiction with a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddha*). According to the principles of Hetuvidyā (Logic), if a valid cognition possesses such a fault, one must admit the use of a statement to exclude it.
Since the valid cognition of the *Tripiṭaka* currently contains this fault, the phrase "admitted by oneself" is placed [at the outset] to exclude it. Question: How can such a fault exist?
Is this a fault? Answer: Within the scope of the Three Piṭakas, although not explicitly stated, it is implicitly intended and contained.

This is because according to the Mahāyāna school, there are two kinds of form (*rūpa*): form that is separate from the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of visual consciousness, and form that is not separate from the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of visual consciousness.
If it is form separate from visual consciousness, the Hīnayāna schools accept it; if it is form not separate from visual consciousness, the Hīnayāna schools do not.
Agreed.

Having already established the correct reason (*hetu*), we shall now examine the statement that sets aside fallacies. Therefore, the Master of the Treatise cites the topical outline and poses a question to clarify the intent behind using explicit language to exclude such errors.

Regarding the "fallacy of contradicting the specific qualification of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha*), this refers to the fourth type among the four types of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*).
This is the fourth type of fallacy, namely "contradiction" (viruddha). Because the subject (dharmin) possesses two distinct meanings, the reason (hetu) contradicts it.
Question: How can this fallacy occur? Below, the meaning of the "distinctness of the subject" (dharmiviśeṣa) is established. Regarding the term "comprehensive" (saṃgrāhaka):
*An* means "to know," which refers to the meaning of mental assent; that is, what is internally accepted by the mind without being expressed in speech is called *an-han* (implicit).
Regarding "substantial form" (*bǐnzhì sè*): this refers to the various sense-faculties and bodies, as well as the physical environment (*bhājana-loka*).

When the eye and the mind take these as objects, they rely upon them as the substance (*pratibimba*), transforming their reflection into the aspect (*nimitta*). Because these exist inherently, they are termed "substantial"; therefore, it is called "substantial."

Regarding the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of form that is distinct from visual consciousness: it arises by relying upon the preceding fundamental object (*ālambana-svabhāva*), transforming a reflected image into the objective aspect.

When visual consciousness perceives form, although it transforms an objective aspect upon its own self-verifying essence (*svasaṃvedana-svabhāva*) as it perceives, because this is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it directly apprehends the essence of the object and does not give rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, with respect to the fundamental object, it only apprehends the objective aspect; this is called "direct" (*sākṣāt*) rather than "perceiving" (*ālambana*), because it is a transformation [of that aspect].
Because it is an aspect (*nimitta*). That which is separated from the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is called a remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭālambana*).

Furthermore, since the aspect of form (*rūpa-nimittabhāga*) and the cognizing consciousness arise as one and the same substance, it is said that the aspect is not separate from the eye-consciousness. The adherents of the Hīnayāna set their intent upon the essential nature;

therefore, they do not admit that form is not separate from the eye-consciousness. They fail to realize that even the essential nature itself has, from time immemorial, been [one with the consciousness].
Since all sentient beings mutually transform [objects] together, how could these exist apart from the mind?

Now, the *Tripiṭaka-ācārya*’s formal inference (*pramāṇa*) states: "True, therefore, the established color is a dharma that exists. If one considers it in terms of the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as expressed by words, this is a color admitted by both the proponent and the opponent;
furthermore, by citing the reason of being "included within the first three [elements] but not included by the eye," it establishes only what is common [to both parties].

It is granted that form is not separate from visual consciousness. If one considers what is accepted by the intention of the Tripiṭaka masters, they merely establish that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of form is not separate from visual consciousness.

Taking as the reason the fact that it is included within the first three [realms] yet not included by the eye, one establishes that the *nimitta-bhāga* of form—which is a specific differentiation of the mental consciousness upon the *dharmin* (the subject)—is certainly not separate from visual consciousness. Therefore, the *Hetuvidyā-ṭīkā* states: "Because it is truly established."

"Form" (*rūpa*) is a phenomenon possessing its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). It is certain that this phenomenon possessing its own specific characteristic does not exist apart from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

"That which is not certain to exist apart from visual consciousness" is a property of differentiation (*viśeṣa*) of that phenomenon. The proponent intends to establish it as not existing apart from visual consciousness.

In this treatise, the author primarily elucidates the meaning of "explicit statement" (*vacana*) and "intended implication" (*abhiprāya*) within the scope of the three criteria of valid proof (*pramāṇa*).

This means that if one looks at the explicit statement regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), only the essential substance (*dravya*) of form (*rūpa*)—which is mutually accepted by both the proponent and the opponent—is presented as the subject (*pakṣa*).

However, when the reason (*hetu*) is adduced to constitute the body of the thesis (*pratijñā*), it also establishes that the mutually accepted essential substance of form is not separate from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). This constitutes the formal proposition (*sthāpanā*).
The opponent and the proponent both allow a *dharmin* (the subject) to serve as the basis for establishing the thesis (*pakṣa*).

However, according to the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) of the Tripiṭaka, this reason (*hetu*) merely establishes a specific portion of the *dharmin*—namely, the aspect of the object (*viṣayabhāga*)—as being inseparable from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Therefore, the *Hetuprakaraṇa-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Reasoning) cites scriptural evidence below to demonstrate that the *dharmin* presented in the thesis possesses such a specific distinction.
Question: When the opponent points out the fault of contradiction with the property of the subject (*dharmin*) in the inference based on the Tripitaka, how can one refute his own statement?

Answer: When the opponent presents the inference that contradicts [the Tripitaka], one uses the two characters "self-acknowledged" (*svābhyupagama*) to point out the fault of the reason being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for the opponent.
Since the opponent's inference already carries this internal fault, what further reasoning could possibly establish the existence of the property of the subject within the Tripitaka-based inference?
Is this not the fallacy of "contradiction through difference"?
Through question and answer, it is clarified that these [objections] mutually entail fallacies and cannot constitute a valid refutation. Question:
What is the form of the contradictory inference presented by the Hīnayāna? Answer: The Hīnayāna says: "At first glance, when examining the words set forth by the proponent..."

Regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): the three members [of the syllogism] are without fault, and upon further investigation of what is established, it is fundamentally understood that if one intends a conceptual distinction regarding the *dharmin* (the subject) and seeks to establish—by means of a reason and an example—that the aspect of form (*rūpa*) admitted by the intention regarding the *dharmin* is not separate from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), then visual consciousness itself cannot serve as the similar example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*).
For instance, visual consciousness is such that there is nothing that is not inseparable from form; because of this, [it cannot be used].

Because all forms are devoid of visual consciousness, and since they are devoid of visual consciousness, they cannot serve as a similar instance (sapakṣa) but instead become a dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
Thus, the reasons such as "being the first three" [of the sense bases] apply instead to the dissimilar instance of visual consciousness. Therefore, the treatise states:

"If there is no locus for the similar instance, the proponent's thesis is not established; if it exists in the dissimilar instance, it conversely establishes the contradictory thesis of the opponent."

Regarding the question and answer herein: it clarifies that when a follower of the Hīnayāna intends to present a counter-argument (*viruddha-pramāṇa*), they must first investigate whether the preceding argument contains faults;
only then can they establish their refutation. That is to say, upon a superficial examination of the stated words, one finds no fault in the three members [of the syllogism];

yet, upon investigating the thesis (*pakṣa*) being established, one knows it contains a fault. If one were then to attempt to establish the "form-aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga-rūpa*) by means of a reason (*hetu*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*)...
Since it is separated from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), one cannot take visual consciousness as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

For example, just as there is no visual consciousness that is not separated from form (*rūpa*), the two consciousnesses of eye and ear apprehend their objects by way of separation. Form and visual consciousness are definitively separate;

being separate, they cannot serve as a similar instance, but rather become a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Thus, the previously stated logical reason (*hetu*) instead points toward the dissimilar instance, the eye.
It turns toward consciousness. Therefore, the treatise states below, citing evidence for the meaning of "contradiction through difference" (*viśeṣaviruddha*).

Since the reasons such as "being the first of the three" and so forth turn toward a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), they do not exist within the similar instances (*sapakṣa*); this constitutes contradiction through difference.

This does not alter the reason established by the Hīnayāna proponent. To state a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) that contradicts it: "The subject is 'form' (*rūpa*), which is truly and universally acknowledged;
the thesis is that it is not non-separate from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). The reason is: because it is included among the first three [bases] and is not included within the eye [base].

The concordant example is like visual consciousness. The application states: "Whatever is included among the first three bases and is not included within the eye base is all not non-separate from visual consciousness."

"Consciousness. The same analogy applies as with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). To say "not" means "non-existent. The Śrāvaka school says: "There is nothing that is not separate from visual consciousness;
form (*rūpa*) is [therein]. This negates the meaning intended by the Tripiṭaka Master, namely, that the *bhāga* (part) of form is non-existent.
Within the *viruddha* (contradictory) fallacy among the types of *pramāṇa*, one does not alter the preceding reason (*hetu*) or the preceding similar example (*sapakṣa*).

Rather, by taking the thesis (*pakṣa*) "not being non-separate from visual consciousness" as being contradictory to the previous thesis, the reason and example follow suit. This constitutes the fault of the *anaikāntika-viruddha* (inconclusive-contradictory) reason.

From the words "Because it is real" (*tattvataḥ*) onwards, the author formally presents the contradictory proof (*viruddha-pramāṇa*). The word "not" (*na*) serves to explain and establish [the contradiction].
This contradicts the previous valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is termed a "reason contradictory to a qualification of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha-hetu*).

For this reason, the Tripiṭaka Master intentionally employed the phrase "admitted by himself" (*svābhyupagama*) to take up the form of the Buddha from another region and thereby establish an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika-doṣa*) against the opponent's valid cognition.
He states the refutation as follows: "Is it like visual consciousness, which is included within the first three [aggregates] yet is not included by the eye?"

Is it not the case that visual consciousness is not separate from the object of visual consciousness? Does this not prove that the "form" (rūpa) you accept as established is not separate from the object of visual consciousness?
Is it like my own position, which holds that the form of Buddhas in other directions is also included within the first three [elements] yet is not subsumed by the eye-faculty?

Since the form of Buddhas in other directions is not separate from the object of visual consciousness, does this in turn prove that the "form" you accept as established is not separate from the object of visual consciousness?
The opponent’s counter-reasoning (pramāṇa) commits the fallacy of "uncertainty for the other" (anyatarāsiddha) within the common [ground]; it is clear that this is not a genuine refutation.
Conversely, the Tripiṭaka’s reasoning actually becomes a genuine proof (sādhana).
This will contradict one's own assertions regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of the Hīnayāna, resulting in the fallacy of being "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

Since the form of a Buddha from another realm is originally asserted by the Mahāyāna itself, and as such belongs to the Mahāyāna, it is likewise not separate from the form perceived by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

Thus, by employing the aforementioned reasons—namely, "being the first three [factors]" and so forth—one establishes that the form of a Buddha from another realm is not separate from visual consciousness, just like those [first three factors].
[The phrase] "and so forth" establishes that visual consciousness is not non-separate from the eye and visual objects; this is a contradictory meaning.

It is also the first type of fallacy among the six types of "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reasons in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*). The passage beginning with "Just as in the case of visual consciousness...

cites the contradictory syllogism (*viruddha-pramāṇa*) of the Hīnayāna. The passage beginning with "Just as in my own admission... presents the autonomous syllogism (*svatantra-prayoga*) of the Mahāyāna, which contradicts the former. This [latter] is inherently...

[Objection: If [the reason] is over-extended (*atiprasaṅga*), it would then invalidate what is not true. Since that [reason] is not true, the authority of the Tripiṭaka would instead become a valid proof (*sādhana*).

[Question: If one does not state "admitted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*) within the reason (*hetu*), and one were to take the form of a Buddha from another world-system as a probans brought forward by the opponent (*para*), which contradicts the externalist's own position, what would be wrong with making this an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*)?
[Answer: If one takes the form of a Buddha from another world-system as a probans without stating "admitted by oneself," [it would be problematic].
This is not accepted by other followers of the Hīnayāna; it constitutes a partial transgression against one of their tenets.

This is because they do not accept that the matter of a Buddha of another direction is included within the first three [realms] or subsumed under the category of what is not perceived by the eye. Therefore, the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra-ṭīkā* states:
If one does not state "admitted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*), then it would be impossible to avoid the fault of indeterminacy regarding the physical form of a Buddha from another direction;

this statement would thus incur the fallacy of being "one-sided" (*anyatara-asiddha*). Question: Why is the term "admitted by oneself" not applied after the opponent has presented a counter-argument, rather than being applied in advance?
Answer: Fearing that it might be difficult [to establish] at the time of debate, one provides this precaution beforehand.
In this context, the question and answer clarify the meaning of one's own accepted position regarding whether or not [the reason] is attached [to the subject].
If one does not attach one's own accepted position to the initial reason, then it would be impossible to claim that the form of a Buddha in another realm contradicts the Śrāvaka vehicle;
for since the latter does not accept the form of a Buddha in another realm as being within the reason, it would incur the first of the four types of unestablished reasons (*asiddha*).
There are two kinds of fallacies. Because [the opponent] does not accept [the reason], this is called the fallacy of "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*).

Therefore, the *Hetuvidyā-ṭīkā* states below that when citing scriptural evidence, one does not say "accepted by oneself," because there must necessarily be the fallacy of being unestablished for one of the two parties. Question: Why is it that [the text] says "not waiting for the outsider" below?
Answer: This indicates that providing prior defense is essential.
Next, regarding the presentation of the question and answer: first, the two characters "because it is real" (*satyatvāt*) have already excluded the fault of contradicting the scriptures.

Why, then, was the term "universally acknowledged" (*prasiddha*) not attached to the subject (*pakṣa*) presented previously? Furthermore, there would be the fault of contradicting one's own tenets (*siddhānta*). Answer: Regarding the two characters "because it is real": [the reason for their placement is as follows].
This merely excludes the fault of contradicting the teaching regarding the essential body (*śarīra*) of the thesis; it does not exclude the contradiction of the thesis regarding its basis (*āśraya*).
If the two characters "universally established" (*prasiddha*) are employed, they then exclude faults such as contradicting the thesis regarding its basis.

Because of the aforementioned fault of confusion between the essence of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and its basis (*pakṣāśraya*) resulting from the previous parenthetical clarification, and fearing that students might find it difficult to distinguish between them, the Master of the Treatise restates the question and answer to explain them in detail.
The two characters "truly" (*satya*) serve merely to exclude the fault of contradicting scripture regarding the essence of the thesis;
for the previous formal argument established "form is certainly not separate from visual consciousness" as the essence of the thesis, yet the world...
The interval is shallow and near. To be born knowing [this] by nature, and for form to exist apart from consciousness—these are points even permitted in the *Āgama* sūtras.
Such views contradict both worldly consensus and the teachings; thus, there is the fault of contradicting both the world and the scriptures regarding the existence of form apart from consciousness.

While the essence of our own tenet holds that form is not separate from consciousness, we now distinguish this by means of "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) because it is true. Therefore, it is said that we merely exclude what contradicts the essence of our own tenet.

Regarding the phrase "the fault of contradicting the teaching" (*śāstravirodha*) and the two characters "universally established" (*prasiddha*): these serve to exclude faults such as contradicting one's own tenets (*svasiddhāntavirodha*) with respect to the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*).
In this context, the subject (*dharmin*) of the first member of the proposition is "form" (*rūpa*), which serves as the basis of the thesis.

The term "form" here encompasses in its entirety the defiled form of Bodhisattvas, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) form of Buddhas, the form of Buddhas in other realms, and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) form of Buddhas—all of which the Hīnayāna school does not accept. Thus, [to assert them] would constitute a contradiction with the tenets of others (*parasiddhivirodha*).
The "particularity of the subject" (*viśeṣya-asiddhi*) is not universally established; this is not accepted by the Mahāyāna, and thus one commits the fallacy of *viśeṣya-asiddhi* for oneself.
If one were to include both schools [the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna] in the subject, one would commit the fallacy of *āśraya-asiddhi* for either one of the two parties.

Regarding the four types of form mentioned above, which pertain to "form as ultimate reality," these are now distinguished by the two characters "universally established" (*prasiddha*). Therefore, it is said:
This immediately eliminates faults such as contradicting the tenet regarding the basis of the thesis.

Question: What is the difference between the subject (the *dharmin*) eye-consciousness and the eye-consciousness used as the similar example (*sapakṣa*)? Answer: Although the eye-consciousness of the subject is the same [as that of the example],...
The intention is that they are distinct. The latter term, "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*), is intended by the author to be the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*).

The common example, "eye-consciousness," is intended by the author to be the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*), because the seeing portion is not separate from the self-cognizing portion, just as within our own school the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is not separate from the self-cognizing portion.
Question: If that is so, why not formulate the syllogism as follows: "The objective aspect is the subject (*dharmin*); it is certainly not separate from the self-cognizing portion..."?

The "perceiving portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is stated as: "because it is included within the first three [factors] yet is not subsumed by the eye. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is "like the seeing portion. Answer:

Because the Hīnayāna schools do not admit that there are four portions, and fearing the commission of a fallacy such as the *anvaya-viparyaya* (contradiction of the positive concomitance), he speaks only of "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣur-vijñāna*).

In the preceding formal argument (*pramāṇa*), both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) were termed "visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Fearing that students might not understand that the names are identical while the meanings differ, this question is raised:
namely, that each of the eight types of consciousness possesses four parts and each has its own respective object of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*).
That which is called the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) each has a cognizing mind, which is called the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect).

Each *darśanabhāga* possesses a fruit-body of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is called the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-cognizing aspect). Each *svasaṃvittibhāga* possesses a fruit-body of direct perception, which is called the *svasaṃvittisaṃvittibhāga* (cognition of self-cognition).

Regarding the subsequent mention of visual consciousness as the *svasaṃvittibhāga*, it is because this is the fruit-body of the eye-faculty; [it is so called] in relation to the two, namely the *nimitta* and *darśana*.
Because the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying portion) manifests as the other portions and is capable of discernment, the self-verifying portion is termed "eye-consciousness.

As for the analogy that the eye-consciousness is called the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*), it is because this is the mind belonging to the eye that is capable of perceiving objects; thus, it is also called "eye-consciousness.
Now, since both the seeing-portion and the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) are inseparable from the substance of that self-verifying portion, [the designation is established] based upon...

The aspect (ākāra) is divided into the objective factor (grāhyāṃśa), while the self-cognizing aspect (svasaṃvittyaṃśa) is included to establish the thesis; thus, the subjective aspect (darśanāṃśa) is used as the analogy.
"If that were so," and so forth, interrogates and clarifies that the Hīnayāna does not admit four aspects, and therefore one cannot establish a thesis based on the name of "four aspects."
Therefore, it is subsequently stated in the subsequent member (*upanaya*) as a common example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Both [the proponent and opponent] speak of "eye-consciousness. Question: By means of this statement in the subsequent member, what kind of form (*rūpa*) is established?
